difficultyReason: The argument has an intermediate conclusion (the drug is effective against the virus in vitro) and an embedded concession (in vivo conditions differ), requiring the student to track two logical moves and match both to the abstract correct answer. Traps exploit partial accuracy.
stimulus: Pharmacologist: A newly synthesized compound has demonstrated strong antiviral activity against influenza A in cell-culture studies. Granted, cell-culture results do not always translate to effective treatments in living organisms, since metabolic processes can neutralize a compound before it reaches target tissues. Nevertheless, every antiviral drug currently approved for clinical use first showed activity in cell-culture studies of this kind. We are therefore justified in regarding the new compound as a promising candidate for further clinical investigation.

choices.label: A
choices.text: citing the uniformity of past successful cases to support an inference that an intermediate step is both necessary and sufficient for a final outcome

choices.label: B
choices.text: acknowledging a limitation of the evidence, then appealing to a pattern shared by all prior confirmed members of a category to support a qualified conclusion about a new candidate

choices.label: C
choices.text: dismissing a counterexample to a general principle by showing that the counterexample involves conditions not present in the case under consideration

choices.label: D
choices.text: drawing an analogy between two experimental methods to conclude that the results of one method are interchangeable with the results of the other

choices.label: E
choices.text: inferring that a compound will succeed in clinical trials by generalizing from the outcomes of a large sample of previously tested compounds

explanations.correct: The pharmacologist concedes that cell-culture results don't always translate (acknowledges a limitation), then uses the fact that all approved antivirals passed through this exact same step (a pattern shared by all prior confirmed members of the category) to conclude the new compound is a promising candidate (qualified conclusion). B captures both moves.
explanations.A: The argument does not claim that cell-culture activity is sufficient for clinical success — in fact it explicitly concedes it is not. 'Sufficient' is an extreme claim the pharmacologist explicitly avoids.
explanations.C: No counterexample is dismissed. The limitation of cell-culture studies is conceded, not refuted. This is the 'dismisses a counterexample' trap.
explanations.D: The argument does not claim the two methods produce interchangeable results; it explicitly notes their results can diverge. This is an extreme-verb / mis-description trap.
explanations.E: The conclusion is qualified ('promising candidate'), not that the compound will succeed. Also, the argument cites a universal pattern (all approved antivirals), not a large sample used for statistical generalization.

difficultyReason: The argument involves applying a principle through a reductio-style move against an opposing claim, with an embedded analogy. Students must distinguish 'deriving an absurd consequence' from 'citing a counterexample,' and the correct answer uses dense formal vocabulary.
stimulus: Legal theorist: Some scholars argue that contracts entered into under conditions of severe economic duress should be enforceable, on the grounds that both parties voluntarily agreed to the terms. But this reasoning proves too much. By the same logic, a person who agrees to hand over her wallet at gunpoint has 'voluntarily' transferred property, and that transfer should be legally binding. Since we clearly do not accept that conclusion, we must reject the premise that economic duress is compatible with the kind of voluntariness required for enforceable agreement.
questionStem: The legal theorist's argument does which one of the following?

choices.label: A
choices.text: appeals to a general principle about contracts to show that a specific case of economic duress is not legally binding

choices.label: B
choices.text: rejects a position by constructing a parallel case whose conclusion is clearly unacceptable, then uses that unacceptability to impugn the original position's premise

choices.label: C
choices.text: cites empirical evidence about how courts have treated duress cases to undermine a theoretical claim about voluntary agreement

choices.label: D
choices.text: argues that because two situations share one relevant feature they must share all legally significant features

choices.label: E
choices.text: establishes a universal definition of voluntariness and then deduces from that definition which contracts are enforceable

explanations.correct: The theorist takes the scholars' logic, applies it to the gunpoint wallet case (a parallel case), shows the conclusion is clearly unacceptable, then uses that unacceptability to reject the premise that economic duress is compatible with voluntariness. This is a reductio-by-analogy move, precisely described by B.
explanations.A: The theorist does not appeal to a pre-established contract principle; the argument works by constructing the parallel case. This is the 'content over technique' trap.
explanations.C: No empirical data about court rulings is cited. This is the 'accurate description of a different argument' trap.
explanations.D: The theorist does not claim the two situations share all legally significant features — only that the underlying logic of voluntariness applies equally. D overstates the move.
explanations.E: No universal definition of voluntariness is established in the argument. The conclusion about voluntariness is derived, not stated as a premise-definition.

difficultyReason: The argument uses elimination of alternatives as its core move, embedded within a causal framing. Students must distinguish 'arguing by elimination' from 'inferring a cause from a correlation' and from 'generalizing from instances,' all of which are plausible-sounding traps.
stimulus: Environmental scientist: Coral reef systems in the northern survey zone have declined significantly over the past two decades. Three hypotheses have been advanced: elevated ocean temperatures, increased sediment runoff from adjacent agricultural land, and overfishing of herbivorous species that control algal growth. Temperature records show no anomalous warming in the northern zone during the relevant period. Sediment levels in the northern zone have remained stable throughout. We are therefore left with the conclusion that the removal of herbivorous fish populations is the most plausible explanation for the observed decline.
questionStem: The environmental scientist's argument derives its conclusion by

choices.label: A
choices.text: inferring a causal relationship from a correlation between the decline of coral reefs and changes in fish populations across multiple reef systems

choices.label: B
choices.text: applying a general ecological principle about predator-prey balance to predict the consequences of removing herbivorous species

choices.label: C
choices.text: eliminating the other candidates from a previously enumerated set of competing explanations on the basis of evidence specific to the case

choices.label: D
choices.text: generalizing from observed declines in a sample of reef systems to all reef systems in the northern survey zone

choices.label: E
choices.text: establishing that overfishing is both a necessary and a sufficient condition for coral reef decline in any marine environment

explanations.correct: The scientist explicitly lists three hypotheses, then eliminates temperature and sediment by citing evidence specific to the northern zone, leaving the overfishing hypothesis as the survivor. This is textbook argument by elimination from an enumerated set.
explanations.A: No correlation across multiple reef systems is presented. The evidence is confined to the northern zone, and the argument's structure is eliminative, not correlational. This is the 'mis-scaled' trap.
explanations.B: No general ecological principle about predator-prey balance is invoked. The argument reaches its conclusion by elimination, not by principle application.
explanations.D: The decline is stipulated as a known fact about the northern zone; the argument is about explaining that decline, not generalizing from a sample.
explanations.E: The conclusion is that overfishing is the 'most plausible explanation' — a qualified claim, not an assertion of necessity and sufficiency. 'Establishes' and 'necessary and sufficient' are both extreme-verb traps.

difficultyReason: The argument contains an intermediate conclusion drawn from an analogy, then used as a premise to reach a normative conclusion. Students must track the two-step structure and the analogical bridge, and must avoid traps that describe only one step.
stimulus: Historian: Scholars who argue that the Athenian assembly was a genuinely democratic institution often point to the fact that all male citizens could participate in debates. But participation in formal deliberation is not equivalent to meaningful political power; modern shareholders can speak at annual meetings without thereby exercising real control over corporate decisions. Since historians agree that shareholder meetings do not constitute democratic governance of corporations, we should equally conclude that the mere right to speak in the Athenian assembly did not, by itself, make Athens a democracy in any substantive sense.

choices.label: A
choices.text: challenging an accepted definition of democracy by offering an etymology that reveals a different original meaning

choices.label: B
choices.text: drawing an analogy to a case whose conclusion is already accepted in order to derive a parallel conclusion about a disputed case

choices.label: C
choices.text: citing historical evidence that Athenian citizens in practice rarely exercised their formal right to speak in assembly debates

choices.label: D
choices.text: establishing a universal principle about political power and then deducing the conclusion as a special case of that principle

choices.label: E
choices.text: refuting the opposing scholars' conclusion by providing a direct counterexample drawn from Athenian historical records

explanations.correct: The historian constructs an analogy: shareholders can speak at meetings but don't control corporations (the already-accepted conclusion), just as Athenians could speak in assembly but didn't thereby hold meaningful power. The accepted verdict on shareholder meetings is imported to settle the disputed question about Athens. This is precisely B.
explanations.A: No etymology is offered. The argument does not appeal to the historical origin of the word 'democracy.' This is the 'accurate description of a different argument' trap.
explanations.C: The argument makes no empirical claim about how often Athenian citizens actually spoke; it challenges the significance of the formal right, not its exercise rate. This is the 'content over technique' trap.
explanations.D: No universal principle is formally established. The claim that formal participation ≠ meaningful power serves as a bridging analogy, not a deductive universal. D overstates the logical structure.
explanations.E: The argument uses an analogy, not a direct counterexample from Athenian records. And the opposing scholars' conclusion is challenged, not refuted by empirical evidence.

difficultyReason: The argument uses a definitional move to rebut a causal claim, embedding that rebuttal within a concession. Students must identify that the core technique is appealing to a definition to undermine a causal inference, rather than presenting counterevidence or a counterexample.
stimulus: Economist: It is sometimes claimed that rising consumer debt levels cause recessions, because high debt burdens force households to reduce spending, thereby contracting aggregate demand. This causal story has intuitive appeal, but it conflates correlation with explanation. A recession, by definition, is a period of sustained decline in economic output. Household deleveraging — debt reduction — is itself a contraction of economic activity. So the supposed cause and the supposed effect are not independent phenomena; they are two descriptions of the same underlying process. One cannot coherently claim that a recession is caused by something that is constitutively part of that very recession.
questionStem: The economist's argument does which one of the following?

choices.label: A
choices.text: offers statistical evidence that correlations between debt levels and recessions are weaker than previously assumed

choices.label: B
choices.text: appeals to the definition of the phenomenon under discussion to argue that a proposed cause and its supposed effect are not genuinely distinct

choices.label: C
choices.text: concedes the empirical accuracy of a causal claim while denying that the claim has any policy implications

choices.label: D
choices.text: identifies an exception to the general pattern of household deleveraging to show that the causal claim does not hold universally

choices.label: E
choices.text: argues by elimination that because debt-driven explanations of recession are implausible, an alternative explanation must be correct

explanations.correct: The economist invokes the definition of recession (sustained decline in output) and the definition of deleveraging (itself a contraction of activity) to show the two are constitutively the same process, making the causal relationship incoherent. This is a paradigm case of appealing to a definition to undermine a causal claim — exactly B.
explanations.A: No statistics are presented. The argument is purely conceptual-definitional. This is the 'accurate description of a different argument' trap.
explanations.C: The economist does not concede empirical accuracy; rather, the argument denies the causal story is even coherent. The move is not about policy implications.
explanations.D: No exception is cited. The argument does not work by finding a case where deleveraging occurs without recession. This is the 'counterexample' trap.
explanations.E: No alternative explanation is offered or argued for. The argument's purpose is to undermine the proposed cause, not to eliminate alternatives and select a survivor.

difficultyReason: The argument applies a general ethical principle to a specific case through a two-step inference, with an intermediate normative claim. Students must distinguish 'applies a principle to a case' from 'establishes a principle by generalization,' and must notice the intermediate step.
stimulus: Ethicist: We generally accept that a person who knowingly benefits from a harm inflicted on another bears some moral responsibility for that harm, even if the person did not directly cause it. Consider now the case of a consumer who purchases goods produced under conditions of forced labor in a distant country. The consumer benefits from the artificially suppressed prices that result from exploited workers. Given that the consumer knows that such conditions exist in the industries whose products they buy, it follows that the consumer bears some degree of moral responsibility for the harms those workers endure.
questionStem: The ethicist's argument derives its conclusion by

choices.label: A
choices.text: establishing a new moral principle about consumer behavior through induction from a series of analogous cases

choices.label: B
choices.text: showing that a consumer who purchases goods knowingly produced under forced labor is a counterexample to the claim that only direct perpetrators bear moral responsibility

choices.label: C
choices.text: applying an accepted general moral principle to a particular case to derive a conclusion about the moral status of that case

choices.label: D
choices.text: drawing an analogy between the economic relationship of consumers to producers and a legal relationship that carries established liability

choices.label: E
choices.text: arguing that because forced labor is widely condemned, any practice that supports it is equally subject to condemnation

explanations.correct: The ethicist begins with an accepted general principle (knowingly benefiting from harm = some moral responsibility), then identifies the specific case (consumer buying forced-labor goods) as satisfying the conditions of that principle, and draws the conclusion that the consumer bears some responsibility. This is a canonical application of a general principle to a specific case.
explanations.A: The principle is not established by induction in the argument — it is stated as a pre-existing, generally accepted premise. The direction is principle → case, not case → principle.
explanations.B: The consumer is not presented as a counterexample to anything; the argument uses the consumer as a new instance that falls under the general principle. No opposing claim about direct perpetrators is under attack.
explanations.D: No specific legal analogy is constructed. The argument operates through a moral principle, not by mapping an economic relationship to a legal liability framework.
explanations.E: The argument does not rely on widespread condemnation of forced labor as its logical engine. The move is from principle about knowing benefit to conclusion about this consumer.

difficultyReason: The argument uses a two-stage move: a counterexample to an opposing universal generalization, followed by an intermediate conclusion that reframes the debate. Students must track both stages and avoid traps that capture only the counterexample move or only the reframing move.
stimulus: Policy analyst: Proponents of mandatory minimum sentencing often claim that such sentences invariably reduce crime rates by incapacitating repeat offenders and deterring potential criminals. Yet jurisdictions that have repealed mandatory minimum statutes have not experienced increases in crime — in several cases, crime rates have actually declined. This is sufficient to show that mandatory minimums are not necessary to maintain public safety. The real question, then, is not whether mandatory minimums reduce crime, but whether the social costs they impose — including prison overcrowding and racial disparities in sentencing — are justified by any marginal crime-reduction benefits they may produce.
questionStem: The policy analyst's argument does which one of the following?

choices.label: A
choices.text: cites instances that undermine a universal claim, uses that to establish an intermediate conclusion, and then shifts the framing of the debate to a cost-benefit question

choices.label: B
choices.text: establishes through a statistical survey that mandatory minimum sentences have failed to reduce crime in the majority of jurisdictions that have adopted them

choices.label: C
choices.text: argues by analogy that because sentencing policy in comparable jurisdictions did not increase crime, it will not do so in the jurisdiction under consideration

choices.label: D
choices.text: applies a general principle about the necessity of incarceration to conclude that mandatory minimums are an insufficient tool of crime prevention

choices.label: E
choices.text: concedes that mandatory minimum sentences reduce crime and argues instead that their social costs are an overriding moral objection to their use

explanations.correct: The analyst first cites cases of jurisdictions that repealed mandatory minimums without crime increases (undermining the universal claim that such sentences are necessary). This yields the intermediate conclusion that mandatory minimums are not necessary for public safety. Then the argument explicitly reframes the debate away from efficacy toward cost-benefit analysis. A captures all three moves accurately.
explanations.B: The argument does not present a statistical survey or claim that mandatory minimums have failed in most jurisdictions. The evidence is narrower: repeal jurisdictions didn't see crime increases. 'Majority of jurisdictions' overstates the evidence.
explanations.C: No analogy to a specific comparable jurisdiction is constructed. The argument's structure is counterexample + intermediate conclusion + reframing, not analogical inference.
explanations.D: No general principle about the necessity of incarceration is invoked. The argument's logical structure is counterexample-driven, not principle-application.
explanations.E: The analyst does not concede that mandatory minimums reduce crime; the intermediate conclusion is that they are not necessary, which is a stronger challenge to the proponents' claim than a mere cost concession.

difficultyReason: The argument uses a structural move rarely tested: distinguishing a token from a type to rebut an opposing inference. Students must identify this type/token distinction as the core technique rather than confusing it with a counterexample move or a definitional appeal.
stimulus: Linguist: Some cognitive scientists claim that because all known human languages share certain structural features — such as the noun-verb distinction — these features must be innately specified in the human mind. But this inference is unwarranted. The fact that all observed instances of a phenomenon share a property does not show that the property is innately determined rather than the result of common environmental pressures. After all, every observed human language has developed in the context of communities that engage in reference and predication, and those communicative demands alone could account for the universality of noun-verb structure.

choices.label: A
choices.text: providing a direct counterexample — a human language that lacks the noun-verb distinction — to falsify the cognitive scientists' generalization

choices.label: B
choices.text: challenging the inference from universal co-occurrence to innateness by offering a competing explanation for the observed universality

choices.label: C
choices.text: applying a general principle about language acquisition to show that structural features must arise from experience rather than innate specification

choices.label: D
choices.text: arguing that the noun-verb distinction is not in fact universal across all human languages, undermining the empirical premise of the opposing view

choices.label: E
choices.text: drawing an analogy between linguistic universals and biological universals to conclude that universality is not evidence of genetic determination

explanations.correct: The linguist does not deny the universality of noun-verb structure, nor provide a counterexample. Instead, the argument attacks the inference from universality to innateness by offering an alternative explanation (common communicative demands), thereby showing the cognitive scientists' conclusion does not follow from the premise. B captures this precisely.
explanations.A: The linguist explicitly accepts the universality premise; no counterexample language is provided. This is the 'counterexample' trap — the argument challenges the inference, not the empirical claim.
explanations.C: No general principle about language acquisition is invoked. The competing explanation (communicative demands) is offered as a possibility, not derived from a principle.
explanations.D: The linguist does not dispute that noun-verb structure is universal — the argument concedes this and attacks the inference to innateness. D directly contradicts the argument's actual move.
explanations.E: No analogy to biological universals is constructed. The argument works by offering an alternative explanation, not by drawing a parallel to another domain.

difficultyReason: The argument uses a nested structure: it identifies what a claim presupposes, shows the presupposition is false, and concludes the claim fails. Students must distinguish this 'undermining a presupposition' technique from a straightforward counterexample or refutation by contradiction.
stimulus: Art critic: The view that digital photography has democratized fine-art photography rests on the assumption that access to professional-quality equipment is the primary barrier to producing art-quality images. But this assumption is false. The most significant barriers to producing art-quality work are not technological but perceptual and conceptual: knowing what to photograph, how to frame a subject, and how to use light expressively. These capacities are developed through sustained study and practice, not through access to equipment. Consequently, the claim that digital photography has democratized fine-art photography is not well supported.
questionStem: The art critic's argument does which one of the following?

choices.label: A
choices.text: surveys the history of fine-art photography to show that the most celebrated works were produced with minimal equipment, thereby undermining the view that equipment determines quality

choices.label: B
choices.text: draws an analogy between fine-art photography and other art forms to argue that perceptual skill is more important than technological access in all creative domains

choices.label: C
choices.text: identifies and rejects a presupposition of an opposing claim, and uses that rejection to conclude that the opposing claim is not adequately supported

choices.label: D
choices.text: concedes that digital photography has lowered equipment costs and then argues that this cost reduction is insufficient to constitute genuine democratization

choices.label: E
choices.text: establishes through empirical evidence that practitioners who use digital equipment produce work of lower quality than those trained in traditional methods

explanations.correct: The critic identifies the assumption that equipment access is the primary barrier (a presupposition underlying the democratization claim), shows this assumption is false (the real barriers are perceptual and conceptual), and concludes the democratization claim is not well supported. C describes this 'undermine the presupposition, undermine the claim' structure precisely.
explanations.A: No historical survey is offered. The argument makes no reference to specific works or periods in photography history. This is the 'accurate description of a different argument' trap.
explanations.B: No analogy to other art forms is constructed. The argument stays entirely within the domain of photography and makes no comparative claim about creative domains generally.
explanations.D: The critic does not concede that digital photography has lowered equipment costs — cost is never mentioned. The argument attacks the underlying assumption about what the barrier is, not the cost-reduction claim.
explanations.E: No empirical comparison between digital and traditional practitioners is presented. The argument is conceptual, not evidential in this sense.

difficultyReason: The argument uses a scope-narrowing move: accepting a general claim but arguing it does not apply to the case at hand due to a distinguishing feature. Students must identify this 'distinguishing the case from the general rule' technique and avoid traps that describe the general rule as the argument's conclusion rather than its premise.
stimulus: Technology policy researcher: Critics of open-source software in government systems argue that because open-source code is publicly readable, it exposes security vulnerabilities to potential attackers. This concern is legitimate as a general matter. However, the government systems in question use a security-through-obscurity model only for their outermost interfaces; the core cryptographic protocols rely on algorithms whose security is mathematically provable regardless of whether the underlying code is public. For these particular systems, then, the general concern about public readability simply does not apply.
questionStem: The technology policy researcher's argument proceeds by

choices.label: A
choices.text: arguing that the critics' general concern about open-source security is empirically unfounded because no government system using open-source code has been successfully attacked

choices.label: B
choices.text: conceding the general validity of an opposing concern but identifying a feature of the specific case that renders the general concern inapplicable to it

choices.label: C
choices.text: applying a general principle about cryptographic security to conclude that open-source code is always more secure than proprietary code

choices.label: D
choices.text: drawing an analogy between government security systems and commercial cryptographic systems to establish that the critics' standard does not apply to either

choices.label: E
choices.text: refuting the critics' position by demonstrating that security-through-obscurity is an inherently flawed model in all software contexts

explanations.correct: The researcher explicitly concedes that the critics' concern is 'legitimate as a general matter,' then identifies a distinguishing feature of the specific systems (their core protocols rely on mathematically provable cryptography, not obscurity) that makes the general concern inapplicable to this case. B captures this two-step concede-then-distinguish structure precisely.
explanations.A: No empirical claim about absence of successful attacks on open-source government systems is made. The argument is structural-conceptual, distinguishing the case by reference to cryptographic architecture. This is the 'accurate description of a different argument' trap.
explanations.C: The researcher does not conclude that open-source code is always more secure. The argument is narrowly about these particular systems, and no general superiority claim is made. 'Always' is an extreme-verb trap.
explanations.D: No analogy to commercial cryptographic systems is constructed. The argument works by distinguishing the case, not by drawing a parallel to another domain.
explanations.E: The researcher does not refute or claim that security-through-obscurity is always flawed — the argument explicitly concedes the general concern is legitimate. 'Refuting' and 'inherently flawed in all contexts' are both extreme-verb traps.
